newsitem.title: UK: Ecu bonds glint as EMU stays in vogue.
newsitem.headline: Ecu bonds glint as EMU stays in vogue.

text.p: International investors are taking advantage of the New Year's renewed optimism over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) by turning their attention to Ecu bonds, analysts said on Tuesday.
Analysts said they were seeing speculative as well as institutional demand for Ecu bonds, noting that recent Ecu bond issues have attracted healthy interest from investors.
"Long term investors are holding it as a convergence trade, but we are quite definitely seeing speculative use as well," said David Brickman at Yamaichi International in London.
"Ecu bonds are the one place that offer good value yield pick-up and it is not justified by the perceived currency risk," said Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi.

For example, at the short end, buying the Ecu BTAN 5.0 percent maturing 1999 versus the franc BTAN 4.5 percent of 1998 provides a yield pickup of about 65 basis points. That has narrowed from more than 80 a week ago, analysts said.
"If you take the view that EMU is on track, then Ecu bonds offer good value," said Brickman.

Analysts at Credit Lyonnais advised selling the franc BTAN 5.75 percent maturing 1998, and buying the Ecu BTAN 7.25 percent maturing 1998. The yield spread is currently about 65 basis points, and Credit Lyonnais has a target of 40 basis points.

The European Investment Bank is said to be eyeing the 10-year sector for an institutionally targeted issue of up to a billion Ecu ($1.2 billion), an issue which analysts said was likely to attract investors.
Also, the spread of benchmark Ecu bonds over Bunds has also narrowed from 35 in early January, down to less than 20 on Monday. It widened slightly to 24 basis points by 1130 GMT.
However, other analysts said there may be little further for the rally to go, as Italian and Spanish bonds have already set new record lows on their spreads against Bunds.

"A lot of the optimism has been on the back of the stronger dollar, leading to a weak mark and allowing high yielding currencies to gain on the core," said David Brown, chief international economist at Bear Stearns in London.
"The upside to the dollar is not unlimited, and at some stage the G7 (Group of Seven) will come in to cap it," he said.
He said interest in Ecu assets could be easily undermined by perceptions that Germany and France were out of step over the role of the European Central Bank (ECB).

France came under fire from the Bundesbank for proposing that countries within EMU should meet informally to co-ordinate economic and exchange rate policies after the launch of the single currency in 1999. Some politicians feared that might undermine the independence of the ECB.

A syndicate manager at a German bank in London said demand for Ecus from institutional buyers was likely to be limited, as fund managers believe they can achieve better returns outside the Ecu bond basket.
"With the basket, you are never going to get the best result, just the mean result," he said. "Institutional money is being managed much more aggressively than that."

He said the EIB deal was more motivated by political ends, than retail demand. Since the success of the Ecu bond market is seen as an issue for progress towards EMU, the EIB has an interest in supporting that market through regular issuance.
Also, with 1.125 billion Ecu in EIB issues maturing over the next few months, the new issue was likely to be bought up by those investors whose existing Ecu bonds have matured, he said.
"The EIB name sells well, the Italians particularly like it, and Ecu bonds will have full covertibility after EMU," he said. ($1=.8520 Ecu)
